meta.title: Unheard: the plane you can't hear
meta.shareTitle: Unheard: your phone names the plane flying over you
meta.description: Drop a video or a sound file: the planes in its sound can sometimes tell where and when it was recorded, and you can take them out. Or hold your phone up and name the plane flying over you.
meta.ogAlt: There's a plane you can't hear. Your phone hears it. Unheard names it. A glowing amber tone bends down across a night-blue spectrogram, as the pitch of a passing plane does.
meta.whereDescription: The hum of the planes in a video or a sound file, matched to a flight archive, can sometimes say where and when it was recorded. Find out, or take those tones out, in your browser: your file never leaves your device.
meta.elsewhereDescription: Make your recording sound like it was made in another city: Unheard puts under your voice the real planes flying over it right now, with the Doppler curves an investigator would match to flight data.

og.sub: Your phone hears it. Unheard names it.

hero.doorText: Your phone can hear a plane you can't: it shows the planes passing nearby, listens while one flies over, and names it. Your recording stays on your phone.

steps.title: A plane leaves a tone
steps.body: Propellers and helicopters hum steadily, too low and faint to notice under a voice. Microphones pick it up all the same, and its pitch falls as the plane passes: the Doppler effect.

steps.title: The curve fits a place and a moment
steps.body: Each flight in the data leaves its own curve at each spot and moment. Unheard looks for the spot and the start time where flights fit the tones in your file, and the search runs in your browser.

steps.title: It works sometimes
steps.body: It takes a plane close enough to leave a trace, ideally two passes, and that flight in the archive. When nothing fits, the page says so, and you can take the tones out of your file.

proof.title: Does it work?
proof.lead: Every change is tested on recorded flybys before it ships. One rule never bends: when Unheard says “It was”, it must be right.

limits: It adds curves. It does not remove those of the planes really over you when you recorded.
Between the polls, each flight's path is dead reckoned. Matched against the true tracks of that minute instead, the added plane is still named in most of our test scenes.
Checked where you really recorded, with the planes of your own sky, Unheard itself can be misled too: one of them may borrow an added curve.
Everything happens on this page: your recording is never sent.

sections.title: When you listen
body: Your recording is analysed on your phone and stays there. The page asks our server for the aircraft around you with your position rounded to about 10 km, and for the ground height and temperature with your position rounded to about 100 m. Unheard saves neither; the host's request logs keep them for a short time. To give the planes their names (airline, route, model), the page asks adsbdb.com about the aircraft around you by their codes, never with your position, and Unheard's server asks planespotters.net for a photo of the one it found, by its code too. Nothing else leaves your phone.
The planes you found are kept in this browser's storage to show your list on the home page. Nothing of it is sent, and Clear removes it.
The language you pick in the menu is kept in a cookie for a year, so the site opens in it next time.
On Somewhere else, the page asks our server for the aircraft over the place you pick, never with your own position, and your recording stays on the page.

A file you open here stays on the page and is never sent. If you use your location to search, it stays on the page too. To search, the page requests the flight tiles of the day and area you search, and tiles of the ground's height for that area from Amazon's open terrain data. A place name you type goes to Open-Meteo to find it on the map, and only that name.

sections.title: When you give a recording
body: Only if you tick the box and press the button. Before anything is sent, your phone rewrites the recording's flight data so it shows the same scene nowhere and at no time: you are moved to 0° 0° at sea level, every aircraft keeps its position relative to you, the whole scene is turned by a random angle so that no runway or approach path gives the place away, the clock is moved to 1 January 2000, and the aircraft lose their address, flight number and registration (they keep their type, such as C172). The angle and the shifts are never sent.

What is sent: the sound (8,000 samples a second, the rate the analysis uses), the anonymised flight data, the temperature, what the page answered, what you said you heard and your note, your browser's name and version, and your microphone's audio settings. Not your location, not the time, not your device's identifiers. The upload goes to a private store; your address is not saved with it.

sections.title: What happens to it
body: Each recording is checked by a program and then by a person before it joins the public dataset the project tests itself on. Parts with voices are cut out. The dataset is published under CC BY 4.0, so anyone may use it with credit.
After sending, the page shows the donation's id. Write to unheard@gwendall.com with it to have the recording removed, before or after publication.

scope.title: What we check
scope.yes: We look for the hum of planes and helicopters whose pitch falls as they pass, between 40 and 400 Hz: the tone that can place a recording on flight data. When we find one, taking it out also takes what we hear higher up, to 3.4 kHz. Jets are harder, their tone sits higher: of four real jet recordings in our tests, we found a tone in three and missed one. Flight data placed two, and neither once cleaned.
scope.no: We do not look for a tone above 400 Hz on its own, for the hum of the power grid (ENF), which can date a recording, or for anything else a video shows or says.

where.offline: The flight archive is not connected yet, so the search is not offered.

facts.nothing: No date or place in the tags we read. GoPros, drones and some other cameras keep GPS elsewhere, where we do not look.
